title: Distributed Caching
summary: Sharding a cache cluster across many nodes and surviving the failure mode unique to caches at scale — the stampede that hits your database the moment a hot key disappears.

slides.markdown:
A single cache node — one Redis instance — runs out of both memory and throughput once a system gets big enough. **Distributed caching** spreads the cache's data and load across many nodes, extending the single-cache ideas from [caching fundamentals](caching-fundamentals) to a cluster.

This topic covers how a cache cluster is sharded with consistent hashing, and the failure mode that's uniquely dangerous for caches: a **stampede**, where losing a hot cache entry sends a wall of traffic straight at the database all at once.

slides.sectionTitle: Why a single cache node stops being enough
slides.markdown:
A single cache node has two hard ceilings: **memory** (it can only hold as much data as the machine's RAM allows) and **throughput** (a single Redis instance tops out around a few hundred thousand ops/sec, no matter how fast the network is).

Once a working set exceeds either ceiling, one node can't help no matter how it's tuned — the fix isn't a bigger cache node, it's *more* cache nodes sharing the load. This mirrors the horizontal-scaling story for application servers, but for a stateful component instead of a stateless one.

The complication a cache adds that a stateless app server doesn't have: each node holds *different* data, so a request has to be routed to the *right* node, not just any node.

slides.sectionTitle: Sharding a cache cluster with consistent hashing
slides.markdown:
The naive way to pick a node for a key is `hash(key) % number_of_nodes` — simple, but it falls apart the moment a node is added or removed: almost every key's target node changes, meaning almost the entire cache is instantly cold and every request becomes a miss.

**Consistent hashing** fixes this by mapping both nodes and keys onto a conceptual ring (a circular hash space); a key belongs to the next node clockwise from its hash position. Adding or removing a node only reshuffles the keys between it and its neighbors on the ring — typically a small fraction of the total, not nearly all of it.

This is the same technique used for sharding databases and content-delivery routing — it's a general answer to "how do I add/remove nodes without a full reshuffle," not something specific to caching.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: cache cluster with consistent hashing and replica nodes
slides.markdown:
![Hash ring of cache nodes with a replica for redundancy](assets/distributed-cache-ring.svg)

Each node owns the arc of the ring between itself and the previous node. A key hashes to a point on the ring and is served by whichever node owns that arc — no central lookup table to keep in sync.

Replica nodes (shown paired with a primary) protect against losing an entire arc of keys if one node fails — without a replica, a node's failure means every key in its arc becomes an instant, simultaneous miss, which is exactly the stampede risk covered next.

assets.alt: Hash ring of cache nodes with a replica for redundancy

slides.sectionTitle: Cache stampede / thundering herd: when everyone misses at once
slides.markdown:
A **cache stampede** (or thundering herd) happens when a single hot key expires or is evicted, and a large number of concurrent requests all miss on it at the same instant — every one of them independently falls through to the database to recompute the same value, at the same time.

The danger is proportional to how hot the key was: a rarely-requested key stampeding is a non-event, but a key backing a homepage or a viral post can see thousands of simultaneous misses turn into thousands of identical, redundant database queries landing in the same millisecond — often enough to take the database down entirely.

This is a caching-specific failure mode: the cache isn't just failing to help, its own expiry mechanism is *causing* the exact overload it exists to prevent.

slides.sectionTitle: Mitigations: request coalescing, jittered TTLs, early recompute
slides.markdown:
Three practical defenses. **Request coalescing** (a.k.a. single-flight): when many requests miss on the same key simultaneously, only the *first* is allowed to hit the database — the rest wait for that one result and share it, instead of each running their own identical query. **Jittered TTLs** add a small random offset to each entry's expiry, so keys that were all set at once don't all expire at exactly the same instant. **Probabilistic early recompute** refreshes a key slightly *before* its TTL, with a small, increasing probability as expiry approaches, so a background refresh usually beats the crowd to it.

None of these are mutually exclusive — production systems commonly run jittered TTLs as a baseline and add request coalescing for the hottest keys specifically.

The shared idea across all three: prevent many callers from redundantly redoing the same expensive work at the same moment.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: client-side sharding vs proxy-based cache clusters
slides.markdown:
Two ways to route requests to the right cache node. **Client-side sharding**: the application itself runs the consistent-hashing logic and talks directly to the correct node — no extra hop, but every client needs to agree on the same hashing scheme and node list. **Proxy-based clustering** (e.g. Twemproxy, or Redis Cluster's own routing layer): clients talk to a proxy, which does the routing — clients stay simple, but the proxy is an extra hop and a potential bottleneck or single point of failure of its own.

| | Client-side sharding | Proxy-based clustering |
|---|---|---|
| Extra network hop | No | Yes (through the proxy) |
| Client complexity | Higher — clients embed the hashing logic | Lower — clients just talk to the proxy |
| Node changes | Every client must learn about them | Only the proxy needs to know |

**How to decide:** client-side sharding suits a small number of trusted, tightly-coupled services; a proxy suits many heterogeneous clients that shouldn't each reimplement routing logic.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a cold cache after deploy causing a stampede on the DB
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Deploying a fresh cache cluster (or restarting one) is safe — the cache will just naturally fill back up as requests come in."

**Why it's wrong:** "filling back up" means every single request in that window is a miss, because the cache is entirely empty. For a high-traffic service, that's not a gentle warm-up — it's the full, unmitigated production load hitting the database all at once, which is often exactly the load the cache existed to absorb in the first place.

**Correct model:** treat cache warm-up as a deployment step, not an assumption. Pre-populate the most critical keys before routing traffic to a fresh cache, or roll the cluster node-by-node so only a fraction of keys go cold at once, keeping the database's load increase bounded.

slides.sectionTitle: Multi-level caching: a local L1 in front of a shared L2
slides.markdown:
A single distributed cache tier isn't the only layer available — many high-traffic systems add a small **L1** cache (in-process memory, per app instance) in front of the shared **L2** distributed cache (Redis/Memcached cluster). L1 serves the hottest handful of keys in nanoseconds with zero network hop; L2 catches everything else and stays consistent across instances.

The cost is a harder consistency story: invalidating a key now means clearing it from L2 *and* every instance's L1, typically via a pub/sub invalidation message broadcast to all nodes. Skipping that broadcast is how L1 caches quietly serve stale data long after L2 has the fresh value.

This two-level design is exactly how CDN edge caches plus an origin cache work, and how client SDKs for cache services (e.g. many Memcached clients) layer a small local cache on top of the network client.
